task: Write one sentence of your own using the word florid. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know florid should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: His thank-you note ran two florid pages when one plain sentence would have done.

Overwrought goes further than florid: the ornament turns to strain, every line overloaded past bearing.

Flowery is the everyday word for dressed-up language, and it is the gentler charge — a few blossoms too many. Florid is stronger and more formal: the whole style is in full ornamental flower, decoration crowding out substance line after line.

High-flown language reaches upward — grand, lofty phrases straining to sound important. Florid decorates instead: curls, blossoms, and perfumed flourishes laid over the sentence. A high-flown speech aims too high; a florid one is dressed too richly, and a passage can easily be both.

Modern editors call the style florid, and the diagnosis fits: the ornament is not an accent but the whole method, blooming in every line until the landscape can barely be seen through the prose.
